title: The Court-Martial of the Captain
lead: You ignored the Admiral's orders, so she has sent new ones, in full dress, by a marine who salutes before handing them over. You are summoned to the Ghostlight to answer a charge of unlawful assumption of command. You may bring counsel, and witnesses. The trial, says the marine, will be scrupulously fair, and you'll find that's the frightening part.

gm.truth: She's right on the law. Under Concord regulations the captain is under her command, and nobody on either side can say otherwise. The court is real: five senior officers in the wardroom of the flagship, polished boots, and an anthem at six every morning. Commodore Lucan Dorn prosecutes, and he's courteous and thorough, and he doesn't want to win. Okonkwo-Reyes doesn't sit on the panel. She's never needed to. Under all the ceremony she has six ships, fuel for two jumps and thirty days of food, and she can't say so, so the trial is also the only way she can think of to get the fleet's fuel and people without asking. The player's real defense isn't on the charge sheet. A commander's legal authority can be challenged only by showing they abandoned their post. And somewhere in known space there's a set of things that say she did: Elsbeth Crane holds the flagship's flight recorder, showing her squadron leaving the line an hour before it broke. Prime Six holds the order in her own voice, telling every synthetic in the line to power down. Rusk's chart shows the same thing, and the sealed order on the CFS Halloway, if it's been found, shows who decided which Meridian lived. Her crews have been told a dead superior gave the withdrawal order. So the captain can walk into a fair trial with a bomb in their pocket, and three thousand decent sailors in the gallery who have nothing else left to believe in. Commander Ilya Voss came up under the Admiral and will be called as a witness. She says almost nothing, and everyone leans in.
beats: The summons, and what it does to the bridge. Going means leaving the fleet for days. Not going means being tried in absentia and every Navy officer in the fleet hearing the verdict.

The Line of Battle: six warships in perfect formation, painted out, and sailors in pressed uniforms, thin as rails. The food on the wardroom table is laid out with great ceremony, and there's very little of it.
The trial. Dorn calls witnesses and reads the regulations. The panel is honest, and two of them are wavering. Voss takes the stand, and looks at the Admiral, and answers one question very carefully.

The captain's defense. They can argue necessity, they can call the fleet's own survivors, or they can put the recorder on the table. If they do, the gallery goes completely silent. The Admiral doesn't blink. She doesn't doubt she was right, and she'll say so.
The verdict, whatever it is. Dorn finds a moment in a corridor to say something very quietly. It leads to the next thread.
routes: Argue the law: lore and persuasion before the panel, with regulations on necessity and acting command, and leadership to speak for thirty thousand people who aren't in the room.
Use the evidence: commerce with Crane, persuasion with Prime Six, or streetwise to find it, then composure and intimidation to decide when and how to play it.
Work the panel: deception and awareness to find which officers are wavering, and what they fear, or to make a private deal with Dorn before anyone sits down.
checks: lore:hard to find a Navy precedent for acting command in a collapse
persuasion:hard to win over an honest officer with an honest argument
leadership:moderate to get three thousand sailors to listen
composure:very_hard to stay level as the Admiral looks at you in open court
commerce:hard to buy a flight recorder from Factor Crane
intimidation:hard to let the Admiral know what you're holding without saying so
fights: remnant_marine, only if the captain tries to walk out of a lawful arrest. Every marine there would be very sorry, and all of them would obey. Losing the verdict never needs to end in a fight.
outcomes: If the captain loses and submits, the Admiral takes command of the fleet in law. She keeps them as captain of the Meridian, because she needs them, and she gives the order for Project Harbor. It's a real change in who gives the orders, and the fleet divides.

If the captain is convicted and refuses, half the Navy officers in the fleet feel honor-bound to go over to her, and the captain is officially a mutineer to anyone who still believes in the Concord. Voss has to decide. Her fate isn't settled here unless the player earns it.

If the panel acquits on necessity, the fleet stands alone with its legitimacy confirmed, and the Remnant is a proud, starving neighbor. Okonkwo-Reyes accepts the verdict, in writing, and doesn't change anything else.

If the evidence goes public, the Remnant shakes. Sailors look at their admiral, and some weep. It's a very strong card and it can only be played once, and it destroys the only thing holding three thousand hungry people together.
gm.rewards: A ruling that either confirms or dissolves the captain's authority, remnant_plate from a sympathetic armorer or remnant_codes if the Commodore starts to trust them, big swings in remnant and fleet standing, and a thin old Navy veteran or two in the fleet who now salute properly.
